questions.prompt: A short story tells how a proud eagle laughs at a slow tortoise, loses a race to it, and admits at the close that patience had beaten speed. The last line prints that lesson for the reader. What kind of narrative is it?

options.text: a myth: gods, and the beginning of the world or of a custom
a slice of life: an hour of an ordinary week, and nothing more
a fable: animals who behave like people, and a moral at the end
a historical narrative: named people who really lived, in a real past

questions.explanation: Two signatures identify a fable and this story carries both: the characters are animals who talk and reason exactly as people do, and the lesson is printed for you in the closing line instead of being left to you. A myth would explain how something in the world came to exist, and gods would be in it. A historical narrative would be tied to men and women who once drew breath, and to things that really befell them, which no race between an eagle and a tortoise ever was. And a slice of life would keep to what an ordinary week actually holds, whereas talking animals are a marvel from the first sentence.

questions.prompt: The old queen's cough grew worse through the night, and before dawn her son sent for the palace physician. Where is the physician a few minutes later?

options.text: on his way to the palace, because he has been called there
at his own house, reading a letter that has only just arrived
in the palace kitchen, where the queen's cook has just fed him
outside the city, because the son has dismissed him

questions.explanation: To send for someone is not to send that person anything: it is to call them to you and expect them to come. The only thing that travels outwards is a message, and the traveller is the person called. That is why the physician is on the road to the palace. Reading a letter would be right if the son had written to him instead of summoning him, and writing is precisely what this expression does not describe. A man being fed in the palace kitchen is already inside the building and needs no summons at all — and note that nothing whatever has been sent to him, which is the commonest misreading of these two words. And dismissing him reverses the direction: sending someone away is the opposite of sending for them.

questions.prompt: A tale opens with this sentence: "The night was so dark that the shepherd lost the path he had walked for twenty years." What is the sentence telling you?

options.text: Losing the path is what made the night seem dark to him.
The darkness of the night is what made him lose the path.
The night was dark, and he lost the path as well, by chance.
The night was dark, and yet he managed to keep to the path.

questions.explanation: This pattern always runs one way. The first half measures something — not merely dark, dark to a degree — and the half after that reports what that degree brought about. The darkness therefore comes first and the lost path follows from it. Reversing the two makes the shepherd's mistake the cause of the weather, which no sentence of this shape can mean. Reading them as two separate facts throws away the whole point of the pattern, which exists precisely to tie them. And nothing here is a contrast: had the shepherd kept to his path, the sentence would have needed a word such as "although".

questions.prompt: Here is a whole story in four sentences. "Every morning for sixty years the women of the village filled their jars at the old well. One July night the well ran dry. On the Friday after that the families began to argue about whose new orchard had drunk the water. In September they dug a second well together and shared it." Which moment is the problem — the one event without which there would be no story at all?

options.text: the sixty years in which the women filled their jars
the Friday on which the families began to argue
the September digging of a second well by both sides
the July night when the old well finally gave out

questions.explanation: The problem is what ends the calm: one occasion, not a habit, and after it nothing can go back to what it was. Three of these four moments carry a date, so a date settles nothing — what settles it is that only one of them turns a quiet arrangement into a quarrel. Sixty years of filling jars is the state the village started from, and a state that has held for sixty years is precisely what a problem has to break. The quarrel over the orchard comes after the break and belongs to the episodes that develop it. And digging a second well together is how the two families put the trouble behind them, which makes it the resolution: it closes the story instead of opening it.

questions.prompt: A chronicler records that the king's treasurer behaved shamefully at the banquet. What is he telling us?

options.text: that the treasurer was far too shy to say a word all evening
that the treasurer acted in a way that brought him disgrace
that the treasurer was ashamed of the food he was served
that the chronicler was ashamed to set the banquet down in writing

questions.explanation: The adverb judges the conduct: to act shamefully is to act in a way that brings disgrace on the one who acts, and it is the chronicler, not the treasurer, who is passing that judgement. The three wrong readings are all close relatives of the word, and none of them will do. Being shy is a difficulty in speaking and carries no disgrace at all. Being ashamed of the food is a feeling inside the man, which may follow bad conduct but is never the conduct itself — one can behave shamefully and feel nothing whatever. And the chronicler's own feelings are not in the sentence: he sets down his verdict on the treasurer's conduct, and says nothing about what writing it down cost him.
